Part 1

Profile verification, safe and pressure-free

How it started

PlanGo is India's first social companionship app for real-world hangouts: movies, coffee, sports, dining and travel. Its promise is companionship without dating pressure.

Strangers meet in real life, so trust is the whole product. Every user must be verified before they can host or join an activity. That makes verification the door to everything else.

Project overview

To keep fake and AI-generated photos out, users took a live selfie that also became their profile picture. Onboarding worked well, but this step made people hesitate, edit and drop off. Two jobs, proof and first impression, were fighting inside one screen.

Design process

We wanted verification to feel safe, not stressful

01 · Usability testing

I watched about 10 users verify their own profile live, thinking aloud as they went.

What users said (translated from Hindi)

“Do I have to take a selfie?”

“Let me step outside and take it.”

“I don't want my photo to look like this.”

Three patterns

  1. Surprise: no warning before the selfie, so people hesitated.
  2. Loss of control: the selfie became their public photo, so many went back to edit.
  3. No choice: gallery uploads were blocked, so users couldn't pick how they looked.
The insight: proof and first impression were the same photo.

Problems for users

Self-conscious: poor light, background, no time to get ready.

The selfie became their first impression, whether they liked it or not.

What this leads to

Extra editing and repeated steps.

Drop-off at the moment trust is built.

Old flow: the selfie was both proof and profile picture

New journey

Separate the two jobs: gallery photos for how people look, a private selfie for proof.

Verified, gallery photos go live

New flow: users submit two photos, then a reviewer compares them

Key design decisions

1. Gallery photos become the profile picture

  • Users choose how they appear
  • Photos only go live after verification

2. The selfie stays private

  • Used only for matching, never shown
  • Removes the pressure of looking perfect

3. Both are mandatory

  • Blocks fake or AI-generated photos
  • Back-end team confirms the same person is in both
Trade-off: Trust vs. speed. Manual matching keeps verification reliable but takes up to 24 hours, slower than automatic checks.

After the review: closing the loop

Review takes up to 24 hours, and users can keep browsing meanwhile. Before, the outcome came only as a push notification, so a missed push left them stuck. I added an in-app card, a profile banner and a tips sheet that lead back into retaking photos.

Why the two in-app messages differ

The push and the profile banner name the exact reason. The in-app card stays generic, because it appears the moment someone opens the app, sometimes in front of others.

In-app card (generic): “Your verification needs another try.” We'd love to get you verified. Tap below to see what to update. Fix my profile

The new in-app path from rejection back to a verified profile

Tension to design around: PlanGo promises fast plans, but review takes up to 24 hours. The app stays fully browsable meanwhile.

Impact

14.8%
Before: 295 of 2,000 signups verified
40.9%
After: 10,233 of 25,000 signups verified
+26 pts
About 2.8x the completion rate

Same paid verification product and same two-month window in both periods. Rates are calculated on all signups. These figures reflect the gallery photo plus selfie redesign; the banners and retake journey came afterwards and are not measured here yet. App-install marketing ran during this time, so this is the result alongside the redesign, not proof the redesign alone caused it.

Part 2

Introducing the chat feature

Meeting a stranger takes trust. Chat lets people talk inside PlanGo before they meet, so trust builds on the platform and engagement stays here. We also explored monetizing it.

How the free limit works

People can send 10 free messages a day. After that, chat locks for 24 hours, unless they unlock it.

0 / 1010 free messages a day
Key design decision: The limit counts messages sent, not conversations, so the rule stays simple.
